findings.source_quote: ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐρῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συνηθείας κολακεύεται καὶ εὐνῆς καὶ ὁ φίλος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς: οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐλεῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συμφορᾶς.
findings.english_quote: Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the merciful person is moved by misfortune.
findings.issue: The Greek carries κολακεύεται through all three members of the analogy by ellipsis. Changing its final occurrence to the neutral “is moved” weakens the shared flattering or enticing image without explaining the change.
findings.suggested_revision: Preserve the shared predicate: “Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune.” Alternatively, consider a consistently applied contextual rendering such as “enticed,” with a note preserving the flattery image.

findings.source_quote: κριτοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἐπιχειρεῖς πράττειν, οὐ τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας σπουδάζεις ἔχειν.
findings.english_quote: you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess humaneness.
findings.issue: The parallel τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας naturally carries forward ἔργον: the work of a judge contrasts with that of humaneness. The draft instead makes the second object the virtue itself. An abstract reading of the elliptical expression is possible, but the source-transparent work/that-of comparison and the reason for departing from it are not disclosed.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider “you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness.” Explain the ellipsis in a note, preserving the alternative understanding “what pertains to humaneness” or its quality. The replacement requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ φαίνονταί τινες ἀγαθοί, ἀθέμιτα κρύφα διαπρασσόμενοι, ἔνιοι δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ὑπὸ διαβολῆς ἐχθρῶν κακοὶ ὑπολαμβανόμενοι.
findings.english_quote: Sometimes people appear to be good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while at other times good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander.
findings.issue: ἔνιοι means “some people,” not “at other times.” The draft introduces a temporal contrast where the Greek contrasts groups of people, and it loses the second explicit qualification “some.”
findings.suggested_revision: Replace the second clause with “while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander.”

findings.source_quote: τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται
findings.english_quote: The good things must come; blessed, however, is the one through whom they come.
findings.issue: The surviving parenthetical φησίν, “he says,” is omitted. The preceding “said” represents ἔφη and does not also cover this separate speech attribution.
findings.suggested_revision: Restore the parenthetical attribution, for example: “The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come.”

findings.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες;
findings.english_quote: For those who, by their own resolve, have advanced in goodness
findings.issue: The supplied προκύψαντες is from προκύπτω, conveying coming forward or emerging. “Advanced in goodness” instead suggests moral progress, the sense associated with προκόπτω, and conceals the supplied verb’s emergence image. The existing notes discuss the punctuation but not this lexical choice.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider “For those who, by their own resolve, have come forward in goodness,” with a note explaining the contextual sense of προκύψαντες. Preserve the printed Greek; no correction to προκόψαντες is warranted by the supplied evidence.

findings.source_quote: τιμῶντες δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν.
findings.english_quote: whereas those who honor them and treat them in ways opposite to how people regarded as wrongdoers are treated show reverence toward God, who has so determined.
findings.issue: The draft supplies a comparison with how wrongdoers are treated. The Greek contains no passive treatment expression supporting that comparison. Even taking τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις as masculine gives “those regarded as doing wrong,” not “how such people are treated.” The note acknowledges the masculine/neuter ambiguity, but that disclosure does not support the added passive comparison.
findings.suggested_revision: Use a defensible comparison without the invented treatment norm, for example the disclosed neuter reading: “whereas those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious show reverence toward God, who has so determined.” Explain the neuter reading and its contextual rationale, while preserving the masculine alternative as a comparison with those regarded as doing wrong, not with their customary treatment. This proposal requires fresh review.
